paragraphs: AUC measures ranking performance, but it is also used to summarize classification performance across different decision thresholds and error costs. This paper examines whether that second interpretation is coherent. The issue is what assumptions connect a ranking summary to the losses incurred when scores are turned into classification decisions.

The criticism addressed by the paper links AUC to expected minimum loss using a distribution over error costs that depends on the model being evaluated. That dependence complicates comparisons between models. The authors establish a different linear relationship between AUC and expected loss, using uniform distributions over both costs and data points that are independent of the model.

The result gives AUC a coherent interpretation under those averaging choices; it does not establish that those choices suit every application. The paper also distinguishes expected loss from loss obtained using only optimal thresholds. For the latter purpose, it identifies the area under the cost curve as a simpler alternative to the proposed H measure.
icml-2011-a-coherent-interpretation-of-a.tldr: The paper gives AUC a coherent expected-loss interpretation using model-independent uniform distributions over costs and data points.

paragraphs: This paper places kernel classification within a framework that combines PAC-Bayes analysis with sample compression. The framework studies classifiers built from compressed training samples and combines their predictions through majority votes. Its scope includes any bounded similarity function, making the treatment applicable to a broad range of ways of comparing examples.

A central result is that the support vector machine classifier is a special case of this larger family of data-dependent voting classifiers. This connects a familiar learning method to a more general construction. The contribution is therefore both a way to understand an existing classifier and a framework for considering other classifiers within the same analysis.

The authors derive new risk bounds for these majority votes and propose learning algorithms that minimize the bounds. This makes the theoretical analysis part of the learning objective, rather than only an assessment applied afterward. The stated contribution links the choice of a voting classifier to a bound on its predictive risk, while retaining the flexibility to use bounded similarities.
icml-2011-a-pac-bayes-sample-compression.tldr: A PAC-Bayes sample-compression framework includes SVMs as voting classifiers and supplies risk bounds that guide learning.

paragraphs: When clustering data, feature selection can either choose one set of useful features for every cluster or choose a different set for each cluster. These global and local approaches reflect different possibilities about which measurements matter. The paper introduces a probabilistic model that can represent both possibilities within one formulation.

The model combines a hierarchical beta-Bernoulli prior with a Dirichlet process mixture model. Adjusting the variance of the beta prior produces global or local feature selection. This gives the distinction between shared and cluster-specific features a place inside the model, instead of requiring a separate modeling framework for each approach.

A variational inference algorithm learns the clustering and feature selections together. The Bayesian formulation also allows the number of clusters and retained features to be learned. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the model can recover both global and local features and cluster data as well as competing methods specialized for each type. The evidence supports the usefulness of a unified formulation across the tested settings.
icml-2011-a-unified-probabilistic-model-.tldr: A unified Bayesian clustering model learns shared or cluster-specific features, along with how many clusters and features to retain.

paragraphs: Rollout classification-based policy iteration uses simulated trajectories to estimate the value of actions and improve a decision policy. This paper studies what happens when those trajectories are cut short and a learned value approximation supplies the remaining return. That additional component is called a critic.

The critic changes how action-value estimates balance bias and variance. Instead of relying entirely on the simulated portion of a trajectory, the estimate also uses an approximation of what comes afterward. The authors argue that controlling this balance can make rollout estimates more accurate and thereby improve policy iteration. The claim is a potential improvement, rather than a guarantee that adding any critic will help.

The resulting algorithm is direct policy iteration with critic, or DPI-Critic. The paper supplies a finite-sample analysis for the case where the critic uses LSTD, tying the analysis to a specific value-estimation method. It also evaluates DPI-Critic against DPI and LSPI on two reinforcement-learning benchmarks. These comparisons investigate the practical effect of supplementing rollouts with a critic.
icml-2011-classification-based-policy-it.tldr: DPI-Critic supplements truncated rollouts with value estimates to control bias and variance in classification-based policy iteration.

paragraphs: A sentiment classifier trained on reviews from one domain may need to operate in another domain where labeled reviews are difficult to obtain. This paper addresses that transfer problem. Its motivation is the breadth of review domains: gathering separate annotated training collections for all of them is difficult.

The proposed approach uses deep learning to extract a meaningful representation of each review without supervision. Sentiment classifiers then use those higher-level features. This separates learning a representation of review text from learning the sentiment prediction itself, with the aim of making training on a labeled source domain useful when the classifier is deployed elsewhere.

On a benchmark covering four Amazon product types, classifiers using the learned representation clearly outperform the state-of-the-art methods considered. The authors also report successful adaptation on a larger dataset spanning 22 domains. Together, these findings provide evidence for both classification effectiveness in the benchmark and scalability across a broader collection of domains. They support representation learning as a practical component of sentiment-domain adaptation.
icml-2011-domain-adaptation-for-large-sc.tldr: Unsupervised deep representations improve sentiment-domain adaptation on a four-domain benchmark and scale to a 22-domain dataset.

paragraphs: In contextual bandit problems, historical records show contexts, selected actions, and received rewards, while rewards for other actions remain unobserved. Evaluating a new policy from these records is difficult because its action choices may differ from those of the policy that collected the data. The observed rewards therefore do not directly represent the new policy.

The paper combines two established sources of information: a model of rewards and a model of the past policy. Reward-based approaches can have substantial bias, while past-policy-based approaches can have high variance. The doubly robust technique brings them together for both policy evaluation and optimization, seeking to retain their strengths while reducing their weaknesses.

The theoretical result supports accurate value estimates when either model is good, without requiring that model to be consistent. This is a qualified robustness claim, not accuracy with two arbitrary models. Extensive empirical comparisons report lower estimation variance and better learned policies, with improvements across the techniques evaluated. The findings connect more reliable historical evaluation to better policy selection.
icml-2011-doubly-robust-policy-evaluatio.tldr: Doubly robust evaluation combines reward and past-policy models, supporting accurate estimates when either model is good.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to turn Dynamic Time Warping distances and similarities into positive definite kernels for time-series learning. The goal combines two concerns: retaining an alignment-based way to compare sequences and obtaining the mathematical structure required by positive definite kernel methods. Computation is also central, since the proposed kernels are intended to be faster to evaluate.

The authors develop new theoretical insights into the existing family of Global Alignment kernels. They use this investigation to propose alternative kernels that are both positive definite and faster to compute. Positive definiteness is thus part of the stated construction, alongside computational efficiency, rather than an empirical property inferred from classification results.

Experiments compare the alternatives with other kernels based on the Dynamic Time Warping formalism. The reported evidence favors the proposed methods in speed and effectiveness for classification. These results support the practical value of the alternatives in the tasks examined. The broader contribution is a way to pursue efficient alignment-based time-series learning while preserving a positive definite kernel formulation.
icml-2011-fast-global-alignment-kernels-.tldr: New positive definite alignment kernels make time-series comparisons faster and show improved classification effectiveness in experiments.

paragraphs: Lasso-TD modifies LSTD by defining its projection step through a Lasso problem. This paper analyzes the resulting value-prediction method with a finite number of samples. It first establishes that Lasso-TD has a unique fixed point and that its algorithmic implementation coincides with the existing LARS-TD and LC-TD methods.

The prediction-error analysis concerns the Markov design setting, where performance is evaluated on the same states used by the method. The authors provide two bounds with different strengths. The first requires no additional assumption but improves relatively slowly as the number of samples grows. It supplies a broad guarantee within that evaluation setting.

The second bound requires the empirical Gram matrix to satisfy a compatibility condition. Under that condition, the rate improves and the error bound explicitly reflects how sparsely the value function can be represented in the available features. The distinction matters: the stronger conclusion depends on a stated property of the data representation. Together, the bounds clarify both general behavior and the circumstances supporting a sharper sparsity-sensitive result.
icml-2011-finite-sample-analysis-of-lass.tldr: Lasso-TD has a unique fixed point and finite-sample error bounds, including a sharper sparsity-sensitive bound under a compatibility condition.

paragraphs: Boosting builds stronger predictors from simpler hypothesis classes. This paper studies that process as gradient-based optimization of a convex objective. It introduces a measure of weak-learner performance that generalizes previous work, providing a basis for analyzing when repeated use of weak learners leads to stronger learning.

For smooth convex objectives, the authors establish weak-to-strong learning guarantees for existing gradient boosting work. They also show that the same approach fails for non-smooth objectives. This distinction identifies a substantive boundary: a guarantee for smooth losses does not by itself justify applying the existing method to every convex loss.

The paper addresses that boundary with new algorithms designed for arbitrary convex loss functions and supplies corresponding weak-to-strong convergence results. Experiments support the analysis and demonstrate the need for the proposed algorithms. The contribution therefore includes both a stronger understanding of an existing boosting approach and an extension that handles a broader class of objectives. The new methods respond directly to the failure identified in the non-smooth setting.
icml-2011-generalized-boosting-algorithm.tldr: The paper proves guarantees for smooth-objective gradient boosting and develops new algorithms with convergence results for arbitrary convex losses.

paragraphs: The infinite dynamic Bayesian network is a nonparametric model for systems with evolving hidden state. Its state is factored into hidden components, and the model can infer the number of those components rather than requiring that aspect of the structure to be fixed. It generalizes the dynamic Bayesian network formulation.

The flexibility extends beyond the number of hidden factors. The model can infer how many values each factor takes, connections among factors and observations, and their conditional relationships. The abstract allows arbitrarily complex connections and conditionals. This expands on earlier nonparametric state-space approaches that generally used binary hidden nodes and more restricted patterns of connection.

The authors demonstrate the new prior on benchmark tests and on weather data and neural information-flow networks. They report finding interesting structure in these settings. The significance is the ability to investigate multiple aspects of a dynamic model together, including hidden-state complexity and relationships between components. The demonstrations support its usefulness for structural discovery without establishing that every inferred structure must match a unique underlying system.
icml-2011-infinite-dynamic-bayesian-netw.tldr: The infinite dynamic Bayesian network learns hidden-state complexity and dependency structure within a flexible nonparametric temporal model.

paragraphs: Learning embeddings from very sparse data can become computationally expensive when the input vocabulary is large. This paper addresses that problem in denoising auto-encoders, which learn representations without labeled supervision by capturing the input distribution. The target applications include word and text representations for natural-language processing.

The main contribution is reconstruction sampling: a procedure that approximates reconstruction error through sampling. The authors show how to construct an unbiased estimator of the training criterion, meaning that the sampled estimate agrees with that criterion on average. This connects the computational shortcut to the original learning objective while making training substantially more efficient.

Experiments on Amazon and RCV1 data demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Instead of shrinking the vocabulary to make training feasible, the approach permits learning with very large vocabularies. On the full Amazon dataset, the reported training-time reduction is a factor of 22. That result is specific to the reported setting, while the broader contribution is a sampling-based way to reduce reconstruction cost when learning from large, sparse inputs.
icml-2011-large-scale-learning-of-embedd.tldr: Reconstruction sampling provides an unbiased training-criterion estimate and reduces full-Amazon training time by a reported factor of 22.

paragraphs: This paper learns a vector-valued prediction function together with a kernel describing relationships between its output components. Those learned relationships have two possible uses: helping prediction and exposing structure in the output space. The method therefore treats the organization of the outputs as something to learn alongside the predictor.

The authors formulate a regularized learning problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of vector-valued functions. Although its objective is non-convex, they prove that it is invex, which implies that every local minimum is also a global minimum. This is a specific structural result about the objective, rather than a claim that it is convex.

A block coordinate descent algorithm exploits the objective's structure by working with blocks of variables. Experiments show that the method can improve classification accuracy, and visualizations provide interpretations of learned kernel matrices on established datasets. These findings illustrate the two intended benefits: predictive improvement and an inspectable representation of output relationships. The empirical claim is that improvement is possible in the evaluated settings, not that jointly learning an output kernel always improves accuracy.
icml-2011-learning-output-kernels-with-b.tldr: Jointly learning predictions and an output kernel can improve classification, with an invex objective whose local minima are global.

paragraphs: Standard max-margin learning for Markov random fields repeatedly adds constraints that the current parameters violate most strongly. Finding those constraints requires exact maximum a posteriori inference: identifying the highest-scoring configuration of variables. For many classes of Markov random fields, that inference problem is computationally intractable and obstructs the learning procedure.

The paper provides an exact inference algorithm for binary Markov random fields with a particular class of higher-order interactions called lower linear envelope potentials. Its running time is polynomial in both the number of variables and the number of linear envelope functions. The tractability result applies to this specified model class, giving a concrete setting where the required inference can be performed.

With that algorithm available, the authors show how to represent the parameters and associated feature vectors within a max-margin framework. This connects the inference result directly to efficient learning of lower linear envelope potentials. The contribution matters because it addresses the computational step needed by the learning procedure and supplies the representation needed to use it.
icml-2011-max-margin-learning-for-lower-.tldr: Polynomial-time exact inference enables efficient max-margin learning for binary MRFs with lower linear envelope potentials.

paragraphs: Output coding tackles multiclass classification by organizing the task into binary classification problems. Existing multiclass boosting methods can learn both a coding matrix and its associated binary classifiers for the problem at hand. The paper describes these approaches through a common sum-of-exponential loss defined over prediction margins.

The proposed algorithm, HingeBoost.OC, instead uses multiclass hinge loss within output-coding-based boosting. Hinge loss is also used in multiclass support vector machines. The contribution brings that choice of training objective into the output-coding boosting framework, creating a different way to learn a multiclass predictor from binary classification components.

The authors evaluate HingeBoost.OC on several real-world datasets against AdaBoost.ERP, one-versus-one, one-versus-all, ECOC, and multiclass SVM. It performs better in a majority of the cases considered. That qualification matters: the findings support the method across many tested comparisons without claiming that it wins every comparison. The results provide empirical evidence that changing the loss within this boosting framework can improve multiclass performance.
icml-2011-multiclass-boosting-with-hinge.tldr: HingeBoost.OC uses multiclass hinge loss in output-coding boosting and outperforms the compared methods in a majority of tested cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiclass prediction when feedback reveals only whether the selected label was correct. After an incorrect prediction, the learner still does not receive the true label. The proposed algorithm builds on the second-order Perceptron and uses upper-confidence bounds to balance exploiting current knowledge with exploring uncertain predictions.

The theoretical analysis uses a partially adversarial setting. An adversary chooses the instances and a linear probabilistic model governing the labels. Under this setup, the authors obtain regret of O(√T log T). Its growth is smaller than the cited O(T^(2/3)) bound for the fully adversarial setting, but the assumptions differ, so the result should not be read as the same guarantee under fully adversarial labels.

Experiments cover nine real-world text classification problems. The authors report state-of-the-art results, including comparisons with online algorithms that receive more complete feedback, with particularly strong performance when label noise is introduced. These findings suggest that the combination of second-order learning and uncertainty-guided exploration can work effectively despite the restricted feedback available to the learner.
icml-2011-multiclass-classification-with.tldr: A second-order bandit classifier achieves O(√T log T) regret under partially adversarial assumptions and strong empirical text-classification results.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning methods can expand their feature representations during learning, but existing expansion methods struggle in high-dimensional problems. The authors conjecture that one reason is poor generalization from features defined over the entire state space. They introduce incremental Feature Dependency Discovery, or iFDD, to create new features in smaller subspaces instead.

The method expands the representation where feedback errors persist. Its design focuses new features on low-dimensional parts of the state space, addressing the proposed generalization difficulty while keeping computation inexpensive. It can be combined with any online, value-based reinforcement-learning method that uses binary features. That compatibility claim is broad within the stated class of methods.

The paper supplies convergence and computational-complexity guarantees and evaluates scalability empirically. In high-dimensional multi-agent planning domains containing hundreds of millions of state-action pairs, iFDD scales well in the reported experiments. The findings support targeted feature expansion as a practical approach to large planning problems. They do not turn the authors' proposed explanation for earlier scaling difficulties into an established universal cause.
icml-2011-online-discovery-of-feature-de.tldr: iFDD adds low-dimensional features where errors persist and demonstrates scalable online reinforcement learning in large multi-agent planning domains.

paragraphs: Online prediction algorithms are often formulated for a single processor, even when data and computation could be spread across several machines. This paper introduces distributed mini-batch, a framework for converting a serial gradient-based online algorithm into a distributed one. The aim is to make distributed execution compatible with strong learning guarantees.

For smooth convex losses and stochastic examples, the authors prove an asymptotically optimal regret bound. Their analysis explicitly includes communication latency between networked computing nodes. This matters because the theoretical account includes the time spent coordinating machines, rather than treating communication as free. The guarantee remains tied to the stated loss and data assumptions.

The paper also develops variants resilient to failures and differences between nodes in a synchronous distributed environment. Applied to distributed stochastic optimization, the method attains an asymptotically linear speedup. Experiments on large-scale online prediction problems demonstrate practical benefits. Together, these contributions connect statistical performance, communication costs, and robustness within a framework for distributing an existing class of learning algorithms.
icml-2011-optimal-distributed-online-pre.tldr: Distributed mini-batching converts serial gradient-based learning into distributed algorithms with latency-aware guarantees under smooth convex, stochastic assumptions.

paragraphs: PILCO is a model-based policy-search method designed to learn control behavior from little experience. A central problem in model-based reinforcement learning is model bias: planning relies on a learned description of the dynamics. The paper addresses this by making uncertainty in that learned description part of long-term planning.

The method learns a probabilistic dynamics model and explicitly carries model uncertainty into policy evaluation. The authors state that this reduces model bias in a principled way and allows learning from scratch in only a few trials. The emphasis is on using the available data while accounting for uncertainty about how the system behaves.

Policy evaluation is computed in closed form using approximate inference, and policy gradients are obtained analytically for improvement. Closed-form computation here does not mean that the inference itself is exact. The authors report unprecedented learning efficiency on challenging, high-dimensional control tasks. These results support the practical value of combining uncertainty-aware planning with analytical policy updates when interaction data are scarce.
icml-2011-pilco-a-model-based-and-data-e.tldr: PILCO incorporates dynamics-model uncertainty into planning and analytical policy updates to learn control policies from very little data.

paragraphs: This paper develops models that connect the text of legislative bills with how legislators vote. The models use ideas from ideal point estimation and topic modeling to predict voting patterns from bill content while inferring legislators' political leanings. This links textual subject matter and political preferences within the same predictive task.

Supervised topics provide a way to explore which patterns in legislative language correlate with political support. That makes the models useful for examining associations as well as making predictions. The stated interpretation is correlational: the learned topics offer a view of how language and support align, rather than demonstrating that particular wording causes legislators to vote a certain way.

The authors derive variational algorithms for approximate posterior inference, supplying a computational approach for fitting the models. Across 12 years of legislative data, they report high accuracy in predicting specific voting patterns. The findings indicate that bill text contains useful predictive information about legislative support, while the inferred leanings and supervised topics offer complementary ways to examine those predictions.
icml-2011-predicting-legislative-roll-ca.tldr: Models combining bill text, topics, and political leanings predict legislative voting patterns with reported high accuracy across 12 years of data.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a broader family of distribution-comparison measures called (f,l)-divergences. These generalize f-divergences while retaining many of their useful properties. The theoretical aim is to expand the available family without losing the properties that make the original measures valuable, although the abstract does not claim that every property carries over.

The framework also gives alternative definitions of familiar divergences in terms of surrogate risks. This connects two ways of describing a comparison: through a divergence and through a risk-based formulation. The contribution is therefore more than a collection of additional measures; it provides a different characterization of established ones within the generalized framework.

As a practical application, the authors derive a new estimator of Kullback-Leibler divergence and use it to cluster sets of vectors. That application connects the theory to an estimation problem and then to a data-analysis task. The stated finding is the construction and use of this estimator. The abstract does not attach a comparative performance claim to the clustering application.
icml-2011-risk-based-generalizations-of-.tldr: Risk-based (f,l)-divergences generalize f-divergences and yield a new KL-divergence estimator used to cluster sets of vectors.

paragraphs: Generative text models often assign a separate word distribution to each class or topic, requiring thousands of parameters even in relatively simple settings. More complex models can also need a hidden switching variable for every token to determine which facet generates it. This paper proposes a different representation to address both sources of complexity.

Each class or topic is represented by changes in log-frequency relative to a shared background distribution. Sparsity can be imposed on those changes to help prevent overfitting. This lets the model describe how a class or topic departs from the background, concentrating its distinctive behavior in a sparse set of deviations.

Multiple generative facets combine by adding their contributions in log space, avoiding token-level switching variables. The authors demonstrate the approach in classification, topic modeling, and more complex models with several facets. Its significance lies in a common construction that supports sparse parameterization and additive composition. These demonstrations establish the idea's applicability across several modeling scenarios rather than a universal performance advantage over other text models.
icml-2011-sparse-additive-generative-mod.tldr: Sparse deviations from a shared background distribution let text models combine generative facets additively without token-level switching variables.

paragraphs: The paper studies choosing k variables from a larger collection to obtain the best linear prediction of a target variable. This is relevant to feature selection and sparse approximation. Its focus is understanding the performance of widely used greedy selection methods, including settings where candidate variables are highly correlated.

The analysis combines ideas from submodular maximization and spectral properties of the covariance matrix. The authors introduce the submodularity ratio as a quantity for explaining greedy performance. They derive what they report as the strongest known approximation guarantees, expressed through that ratio and the smallest k-sparse eigenvalue. They also substantially improve existing guarantees for greedy dictionary selection.

Experiments on real and synthetic datasets complement the theoretical results. In these tests, the submodularity ratio predicts greedy performance better than the other spectral parameters examined. This gives the new quantity both a role in formal guarantees and an empirical interpretation. The contribution helps explain why greedy methods can succeed with correlated variables, without claiming that correlation is harmless in every selection problem.
icml-2011-submodular-meets-spectral-gree.tldr: The submodularity ratio sharpens guarantees for greedy selection and empirically predicts performance better than the spectral parameters compared.

paragraphs: This paper shows that a support vector machine can be interpreted as a maximum likelihood estimate within a class of probabilistic models. The result connects the SVM learning procedure to probabilistic estimation. Its central contribution is a different mathematical view of the classifier and of the model family that it represents.

The authors describe that family as a reparameterization of the SVM, drawing an analogy with the way the nu-SVM reparameterizes the original formulation. The probabilistic model is not discriminative and has a non-uniform marginal distribution. Those properties are part of the proposed interpretation, so the result should not be reduced to the claim that the SVM simply learns conditional class probabilities.

To illustrate the usefulness of the perspective, the paper re-derives and re-examines two established SVM-related algorithms. This makes the interpretation operational: it supplies a framework for revisiting existing procedures as well as describing the SVM itself. The stated benefit is a new route to understanding those algorithms, with no empirical performance improvement asserted in the abstract.
icml-2011-support-vector-machines-as-pro.tldr: The SVM is recast as maximum likelihood estimation in a non-discriminative probabilistic model family with a non-uniform marginal.

paragraphs: Diffusion data often reveal when nodes adopt information or become infected without revealing who transmitted to whom. This paper uses those observed times to infer both the network's edges and the transmission rate associated with each edge. It therefore seeks to recover connectivity and the timing dynamics of spread together.

The model represents a discrete network with continuous-time transmission processes operating at different rates. It selects edges and rates that best explain the observed cascades through a convex optimization problem. The formulation naturally produces sparse solutions and, as stated in the abstract, requires no parameter tuning. Sparsity follows from the model rather than an added heuristic.

The optimization separates into independent smaller problems, supporting networks with hundreds of thousands of nodes. Experiments on real and synthetic data show recovery of network edges and accurate estimates of their transmission rates. These findings support using cascade timing to reconstruct otherwise hidden diffusion dynamics. Such reconstruction provides information relevant to forecasting and influencing spread, which motivates the problem.
icml-2011-uncovering-the-temporal-dynami.tldr: A scalable convex model infers diffusion-network edges and transmission rates from observed cascade times.

paragraphs: A spike-and-slab restricted Boltzmann machine pairs a binary spike variable with a real-valued slab variable in each hidden unit. This paper extends that image-modeling framework in two ways, aiming to improve its ability to learn useful features while strengthening the mathematical definition of its conditional distributions.

The first change allows the observed variables to have nonzero conditional means given the binary spikes. The second introduces a term quadratic in the observed data. The authors use that term to guarantee that all of the model's conditional distributions are well defined, a guarantee absent from the original formulation. These changes expand the model while addressing a specific mathematical issue.

The generalized model improves feature-learning performance and achieves competitive results on CIFAR-10 image classification. In a convolutional configuration, it also generates sensible image samples. The authors interpret those samples as evidence that the model has captured broad statistical structure in natural images. The classification and generation findings provide complementary evidence about its learned representation, without claiming that it captures every aspect of image structure.
icml-2011-unsupervised-models-of-images-.tldr: An extended spike-and-slab RBM guarantees well-defined conditionals, improves feature learning, and generates images reflecting broad natural-image structure.
